slides.title: From ASR to Conversational AI
slides.text:
From ASR to Conversational AI
•  Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) acts as the ear, converting acoustic signals
   into text by breaking speech into phonemes (sounds) and mapping them to text.
•  Simply converting sound to text does not mean the machine actually
   understands the meaning of the words.
•  The Role of Conversational AI: Conversational AI acts as the brain.
•   It takes the raw text output from the ASR and uses Natural Language Processing
   (NLP) to extract the user's underlying intent.

•  While ASR answers the question, "What words did the
   user say?", Conversational AI answers the question,
   "What does the user want me to do, and how should I
   respond?"



                                                                                                           3

visualInspection.notes: ASR ear versus conversational AI brain analogy actually viewed. ASR waveform→text; conversational system extracts intent and response with NLP. Phoneme decomposition is presented as if universal but modern direct systems need not expose phoneme stages. Avoid literal cognitive or consciousness claims.

slides.title: Inspiration behind chatbots
slides.text:
Inspiration behind chatbots
•  The Turing Test proposed by Alan Turing in 1950 to evaluate whether a machine
   can exhibit human-like conversational behaviour.
•  The Imitation Game: A human judge communicates
   through text with a human and a machine. If the judge
   cannot distinguish the machine from the human, the
   machine is said to have passed the Turing Test.
•  The Turing Test inspired the development of chatbots,
   Conversational AI, virtual assistants & social robots.
•  Limitation: Passing the Turing Test does not mean the
   machine truly understands language or emotions.
    –  Early researchers attempted to pass the Turing Test using
       simple rule-based conversational systems, leading to the
       development of the first chatbots.

                                                                                                           5

visualInspection.notes: All Turing Test bullets and diagram viewed. Human judge exchanges text with hidden human and hidden AI; distinguishability criterion;1950 attribution. Behavioral test does not establish internal understanding or emotions. This is a simplified test description, not a rigorous numerical pass-rate protocol.

INPUTIntroduction to chatbots                                   Chatbot/Voice
•  A chatbot is a software system designed to                          Assistant
   communicate with humans using natural language                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           OUTPUT   through text or speech.
•   It understands user input, generates an appropriate
   response and maintains a conversation.
•  A chatbot can be rule-based (ELIZA), retrieval-based

   (ChatGPT), or integrated as a digital voice assistant

•  A chatbot serves as the communication layer between

slides.title: Rule-based chatbots
slides.text:
Rule-based chatbots
•  Rule-based chatbots generate responses
   using predefined rules written by developers,
   following a simple IF-THEN logic.
•  They do not learn from data and do not                            THENIF responseinput = "hello"= "Hello!
   understand language.                                                   How can I help you?"
•   It’s simple to build and it is predictable, thus
   making it ideal for fixed tasks.
•   It is not suitable for modern-day robots because it can
   neither understand context nor handle unseen questions.
•   It lacks reasoning capacity.
•  Instead of manually writing thousands of rules, can we
   build systems that learn patterns directly from data?


                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Rule-based bullets and entire yes/no flow viewed. UserInput→PatternMatching→RuleFound? yesReturnResponse/noSorryIdidnotgetyou. Exact hello IF–THEN response. Fixed developer rules/no data learning describes pure fixed rules; broad unsuitable for modern robots/no context/no unseen questions overclaim because rules can carry state/wildcards and constrained tasks.

slides.title: ELIZA: The Original Rule-Based Conversation Engine
slides.text:
ELIZA: The Original Rule-Based Conversation Engine
•  Invented in 1964 by MIT professor Joseph Weizenbaum, ELIZA is considered the
    original conversational engine software.
•  The core program was not hardcoded for therapy; it
   relied on swappable text files that contained all the
    rules, synonyms, and keywords for forming replies.
•  Instead of generating new ideas, it reflected the
   patient's words back at them, making it an ideal
   candidate for a pattern-matching system.
•  This rule-based script data eventually evolved into the
   modern Artificial Intelligence Markup Language (AIML)
   used in expert systems.
•  Limitation: The system had no context memory beyond
   the immediate previous statement.

                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: ELIZA history, swappable script architecture and screen dialogue read. User I hate cats → You say you hate cats?; Yes → You seem to be quite positive. Therapy is a script rather than hardcoded core.1964 and no memory beyond immediate statement require original-source check; original MEMORY facility may be relevant, not modern coherent context.

slides.title: Retrieval-based chatbots
slides.text:
Retrieval-based chatbots
•  Retrieval-based chatbots search a predefined knowledge base and retrieve the
   most relevant response to the user's query.



•  Instead of looking for an exact match, retrieval-based chatbots search for the
   most similar question in their knowledge base.
•  Sentences with similar meanings are placed closer together in the vector space.
•  Limitation: Since it cannot generate new information, it
  may fail when no similar question exists.
•  What if a robot must generate a completely new response
   that has never been written before?


                                                                                                          10

visualInspection.notes: Five-box vector retrieval diagram and text viewed: UserQuery→ConvertQueryintoVector→SimilaritySearch→RetrieveBestMatchingResponse→ReturnResponse. Similar rather than exact question; fixed response bank limits novelty. Embedding proximity model dependent; not every retrieval system uses vectors. No distances/threshold/numerical coordinates supplied.

slides.title: ALICE (Artificial Linguist Internet Computer Entity)
slides.text:
ALICE (Artificial Linguist Internet Computer Entity)
•  As computer programs evolved, the basic pattern-matching concepts of
   ELIZA were amplified into a general-purpose software entity called ALICE
    (Artificial Linguist Internet Computer Entity).
•  ALICE relies on a massive database of stored phrases and words, using
   decision-making software to retrieve the most appropriate reply.
•   It retains ELIZA's core concepts, such as pre- and post-substitution of
   words, keyword recognition, and response patterns, but scales them to
   cover far more subjects and capabilities.
•  ALICE is open-source software and its architecture is
    still used today to build robot personalities and
   conversational agents.


                                                                                                          11

visualInspection.notes: ALICE expansion and all text viewed: Artificial Linguist Internet Computer Entity; database phrases, pre/post substitutions, keywords and response patterns, broader subjects. Open-source/current-use prose time dependent; pattern-rule architecture not automatically the preceding dense-vector similarity pipeline.

slides.title: AIML – The Language of Retrieval
slides.text:
AIML – The Language of Retrieval
•  To scale up from ELIZA's simple text files, developers created AIML (Artificial
   Intelligence Markup Language), an XML-based language that forms the database
   for ALICE.
•  Developers program retrieval rules using specific tags to link human inputs to
   robot outputs:
    – <category>: Defines the basic unit of conversational knowledge
    – <pattern>: The trigger text or keyword pattern the robot listens for, from the user
   ꟷ<template>: The programmed response the robot will
        retrieve and speak back
   ꟷ<think>: A hidden tag that allows the robot to store
        context or variables (like setting the topic of conversation)
       without speaking them aloud



                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: AIML expansion Artificial Intelligence Markup Language, XML foundation and category/pattern/template/think tags viewed. Category is the basic unit; pattern is the input trigger; template supplies the response; think hides evaluated variable/context operations. Think suppresses rendered output; setters perform state change.

slides.title: AIML – Code Example 1
slides.text:
AIML – Code Example 1
•  Example 1: Direct Pattern Matching





•    If a user types "I play my guitar", the wildcard (*) captures the phrase.
•  <person/>: This tag acts as a post-processing filter. It swaps the pronoun
   “my” for “your” so the robot outputs "your guitar".
• <set_it>: This tag solves the memory limitation of
   early systems. It quietly saves "your guitar" into the
   robot's context memory under the variable "it", allowing
  the robot to track the subject for the next sentence


                                                                                                          13

visualInspection.notes: Full code and prose viewed. Input I play my guitar.; pattern I PLAY *; template Is <set_it><person/></set_it> a game or a musical instrument? Wildcard captures my guitar; supplied person substitution gives your guitar. Legacy-style set_it both returns its value inside the visible reply and stores it under the explicitly supplied semantics. The prose saying quietly saves does not imply the enclosing visible response is suppressed. Runtime and normalization are unspecified.

slides.title: AIML – Code Example 2
slides.text:
AIML – Code Example 2
•  Example 2: Remembering Context





•  The user types "I read Sci-Fi books." The robot replies, "Name some books in that genre“
•  <think>:executes hidden actions by storing "read Sci-Fi books"
   as the new conversational topic (<settopic>), and it even
   changes its own internal state variable to shift its artificial
   personality to "critical" (<set_personality>)
•  Advantage: This retrieval method is highly predictable and safe
   for robotics, ensuring the machine always gives a structured,
   developer-approved answer

                                                                                                          14

visualInspection.notes: Full code viewed. Input I read Sci-fi books.; pattern I READ * BOOKS; visible Name some books in that genre. Hidden nested set_it/set_does/settopic stores read <person/> books, and a second think sets personality to critical. Case of Sci-fi varies in prose. All five legacy-style setters need explicit semantics rather than being silently changed to modern AIML. Predictability and developer approval do not establish safety for all wildcard input or robot actions.

slides.title: 3. Generative Chatbots
slides.text:
3. Generative Chatbots
•  Unlike retrieval-based chatbots, generative chatbots
   do not select a response from a predefined database.
•  Instead, they generate a new response one
   token (word/subword) at a time using a model.
•  The model predicts the most probable next
   token based on the context.
•  The model selects a token and repeats the
   process until a complete response is generated.
•  Modern generative chatbots are powered by Large
   Language Models (LLMs), which use Transformer
   architectures to generate responses token-by-token.
• We have discussed Transformers in the previous lecture.


                                                                                                          15

visualInspection.notes: All prose and User Input to Generative AI Model to response diagram viewed. Generative models compose output token by token, including word or subword tokens; most probable is a greedy decoding description, not every possible decoding policy. Context is finite rather than an unlimited memory guarantee.

slides.title: Beyond Chatbots: Voice Assistants
slides.text:
Beyond Chatbots: Voice Assistants
•  The Naive Pipeline: Standard digital voice assistants rely on a three-part
   sequential pipeline, commonly called ASR → LLM → TTS
   – Speech-To-Text (STT) Module (already discussed in the ASR lecture)
   – Response Generation by an LLM
   – Text-to-Speech (TTS) Module
•   All three modules are either set up offline (via open source)/online (via API credits)
   – Open-source examples: Whisper (STT) → Ollama/Llama 3 (LLM) → Piper (TTS)
   – Online examples: Google Cloud STT → OpenAI API
       (GPT) → Google Cloud TTS
•  Limitations: information loss (discarding paralinguistic
   tone and emotion), high latency, and cumulative errors
   cascading from the ASR module to the LLM.


                                                                                                          17

visualInspection.notes: All sequential boxes and online/offline examples viewed. Offline Whisper to Ollama/Llama 3 to Piper; online Google Cloud STT to OpenAI API GPT to Google Cloud TTS. Ollama is a runtime, Llama a model. Text bottleneck can lose acoustic cues; delays and upstream errors can propagate. Offline/online are example stacks, not mandatory all-or-none deployment.

slides.title: Commercial Voice Assistants
slides.text:
Commercial Voice Assistants
•  While marketed as digital assistants, devices like Siri, Alexa, and Google Assistant
   are technically intent-driven, retrieval-based chatbots.                      Siri     Alexa
•  A local wake-word engine detects the trigger and sends the
   recorded audio to a cloud speech-to-text service for transcription
•  An NLP system processes the transcribed text to remove filler   Google
   words and determine the user's intended command.             Assistant
•  After identifying the intent, the assistant performs the required action,
   retrieves a predefined response, and converts it to speech using a TTS engine.
•  They are optimized for short-turn dialogues and operate
   with minimal contextual memory.
•  While virtual assistants only execute digital software calls,
  an embodied robotic assistant must bridge this identical
   linguistic pipeline directly to a physical control loop.

                                                                                                          18

visualInspection.notes: All numbered steps viewed: local wake word, cloud audio/STT, NLP intent, action or predefined response, TTS. Slide broadly labels named assistants retrieval systems with minimal context. Treat as a simplified historical architecture, not an exhaustive current product claim. Software versus physical action distinction is contextual; software assistants can invoke connected physical devices.

slides.title: Stages in Robot Speech Recognition
slides.text:
Stages in Robot Speech Recognition
•  Unlike cloud servers, most mobile robots have limited
   onboard computing power to run robust, continuous
   Speech-to-Text (STT) engines.
•  They rely on edge devices like Raspberry Pi, Jetson Orin
  Nano etc
•  Modern robots split the task into two stages:
    – Wake word Recognition: They listen continuously for a
       simple wake word, like Hello robot, using local processing.
       At this stage, the robot isn’t recording anything.
    – ASR: To process complex commands, switch to a cloud-
       based STT engine (like Google Cloud)/ download whisper
       STT model to use it locally.



                                                                                                          19

visualInspection.notes: Actual figure shows continuously listening robot and activated Hello robot; text names Raspberry Pi and Jetson Orin Nano as edge examples. Local wake-word monitoring precedes cloud or local full STT. Not recording anything is ambiguous: monitoring still samples/processes audio, while durable recording and upload are separate choices.

slides.title: Robot Voice Assistant Pipeline
slides.text:
Robot Voice Assistant Pipeline
•  Robots use voice assistants to understand human commands, answer questions,
   and assist with task planning.
•  Communication begins with sequential
    (yellow boxes) natural language processing:
   ꟷ  Intent parsing: The text from STT is
        immediately filtered to strip away
        conversational filler, mapping key nouns &
        verbs to a registered programmatic intent.
•  Once the target response & intent are formulated, the pipeline splits into two
   simultaneous paths (blue boxes) to ensure immediate
   real-time execution:
   ꟷThe generated text is passed to the TTS engine to output
        synthesised verbal feedback.
   ꟷThe extracted intent is dispatched directly to the ROS State
       Machine, triggering instant physical Robot Action.

                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: All figure arrows traced: user to STT to Intent Parsing to LLM; LLM branches to TTS back to user and ROS State Machine to Robot Action. Yellow boxes sequential; blue branches may run concurrently. Diagram does not establish zero latency, safe motion, exact scheduling or executable validation. Lower text ends with instant physical Robot Action.

slides.title: From Words to Meaning: Intent Parsing
slides.text:
From Words to Meaning: Intent Parsing
•  Once STT provides a text string, the robot must figure out what to do.
•  Human commands can vary for the same task
•  To clean a room, a human might say: "Let's clean up this room," "Put away the
   toys," "Pick up all the toys," or "Time to clean up“
•  The robot must use NLP to parse the intent of the speaker so that any of these
   reasonable sentences map to a single " clean a room " executable program.





                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: All four prose commands and three speech bubbles viewed. Clean up this room, Pick up the toys, Put those away converge on Execute Clean-up Program. This is a supplied task mapping, not universal synonymy: scope and referents can differ.

slides.title: Keyword Extraction for Intent
slides.text:
Keyword Extraction for Intent
•  To deduce intent, robots can filter out
  common conjunctions and pronouns to focus
   on keywords.
    –  "Could you please pick up all the toys" reduces
        to “pick toys"
    – "Can you clean this room" reduces to “clean
      room“
•  Because words like "clean" or "toys" don't relate to other
   robotic functions (like "turn left"), the robot can
   accurately associate these keywords with the specific
   intent to start cleaning.
•  After keyword extraction, the rest of the pipeline is
   similar to the naive voice assistant, except that it includes
   action execution along with robot speech.

                                                                                                          22

visualInspection.notes: Text examples retain pick toys and clean room. Figure striking out Could you please, up, all the leaves pick/toys, although up is printed bold under strike. Unique keywords cannot guarantee correct intent if negation, object reference or scope is discarded. Robot speech and action are distinct downstream outputs.

slides.title: Limitations of Voice Assistants
slides.text:
Limitations of Voice Assistants
•   Traditional conversational robots rely on an "ASR + LLM + TTS" pipeline.
•  This staged approach suffers from three major flaws:
    –  Information Loss: Converting speech to text strips away crucial paralinguistic
       information (pitch, timbre, tonality, and emotion).
    –  Significant Latency: Running three complex modules sequentially creates unnatural
        conversational delays.
    – Cumulative Error: Transcription errors from the ASR module cascade into the LLM,
        resulting in incorrectly generated responses.
•  The Solution: Modern systems are shifting to Speech
   Language Models (SpeechLMs), autoregressive
   foundation models that process and generate speech
   end-to-end without needing to convert it to text first.



                                                                                                          23

visualInspection.notes: Three flaws viewed: lost pitch/timbre/tonality/emotion cues, sequential latency, ASR errors propagating. SpeechLMs can process/generate speech without a mandatory transcript bottleneck. End-to-end does not guarantee zero error, zero delay, or universal full duplex.

slides.title: How Speech Language Models Work?
slides.text:
How Speech Language Models Work?
•  SpeechLM Architecture: Instead of text, these models use an End-to-End
   architecture consisting of three components:
    – Speech Tokenizer: Encodes continuous audio waveforms directly into discrete or
       continuous tokens
    – Language Model: Uses a transformer architecture to autoregressively predict the
       next speech token based on the context
    –  Vocoder: Synthesizes the generated speech tokens back into an audio waveform





                                                                                                          24

visualInspection.notes: Every component and multimodal arrow viewed. Speech tokenizer maps waveform to discrete or continuous tokens; transformer autoregressively predicts next speech token; vocoder returns waveform. Figure also shows text input/output paths and cross-modal arrows. Input The quick brown fox jumps over and output the lazy dog. are continuations; transcript captions explain content, not necessarily mandatory internal ASR.

slides.title: Speech Language Models - Advantages
slides.text:
Speech Language Models - Advantages
•  Preserving Emotion (Paralinguistics): This allows the robot to accurately interpret
   user intent based on tone and generate highly expressive speech.
•  The Token Trade-Off: Semantic tokens capture meaning well but lose high-
   frequency acoustic details, while acoustic tokens retain high-fidelity audio but can
   struggle with content inaccuracies.
    – Advanced SpeechLMs use mixed tokens to balance both
•  Full-Duplex Interaction: Because they process audio continuously, advanced
   SpeechLMs enable true real-time interaction, meaning the robot can listen while
   speaking, handle human interruptions naturally, and
   recognize when it is appropriate to stay silent.
•  Example: OpenAI Realtime Models
•    If tone and emotion are preserved in Speech-to-Speech
   systems, can robots begin to understand human emotions as well?

                                                                                                          25

visualInspection.notes: All bullets viewed: semantic tokens favor content but lose acoustic detail; acoustic tokens preserve fidelity but may struggle with content; mixed tokens balance goals. Full duplex permits listening during speech and interruption handling in suitably designed systems. OpenAI Realtime named only as source example. Preserved cues do not guarantee correct intent/emotion inference.

slides.title: Lack of Emotionally Aware Voice Assistants
slides.text:
Lack of Emotionally Aware Voice Assistants

•  The Loss of Affective Cues: Early chatbots and traditional speech recognition
   systems focused exclusively on what was said, treating the subtle qualities of how
     it was said, such as pitch, rhythm, and vocal intonation, as merely noise.
•  The Problem of Internal States: Because true affective states are internal, these
   early systems had no way to infer a user's feelings, track emotional context over
   time, or adapt to the human's mood.
•  The Need for Artificial Personality: To make Human-Robot Interaction feel truly
   natural and engaging, a robot must be able to simulate a
   dynamic personality and react to emotional cues, even
   though robots do not possess actual feelings or biological
   needs.




                                                                                                          26

visualInspection.notes: All three bullets viewed: loss of how speech was said, internal affective states, dynamic simulated personality. No way to infer is too strong if interpreted universally: hidden states are not directly measured, but observations may support uncertain inference. Simulated responses do not by themselves establish subjective feelings.

slides.title: Towards Emotion-aware Robots
slides.text:
Towards Emotion-aware Robots
•  Today's robots can recognize emotional signals reasonably well.
•  However, they cannot truly understand human emotions the way humans do.
•  The Third-Person Observer: Since a robot is an external observer that cannot
   read minds, it must learn to recognize emotions by treating them as a pattern
   recognition problem based on observable external functions, such as facial
   motion and speech patterns.
•  Emotional AI remains one of the major unsolved challenges in Human-Robot
   Interaction.
•  Building the models to recognize these multi-modal
   patterns is how we create the Robot Emotion Engine





                                                                                                          27

visualInspection.notes: All five bullets viewed. Facial motion and speech patterns are observable cues used for pattern recognition; emotion engine combines modalities. Recognize reasonably well and cannot truly understand are broad evaluative claims, not supplied metrics or operational definitions. Questions will test external evidence and uncertainty, not assert a consciousness theorem.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary
•  Conversational AI has progressed from simple rule-based scripts (ELIZA) and
    retrieval systems (ALICE) to powerful, context-aware Generative AI capable of
   sustaining multi-turn dialogues.
•  True Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) goes beyond simply transcribing text; it
   requires parsing the user's underlying intent and maintaining a Context Memory
   to act as an artificial personality.
•  The naive ASR + LLM + TTS pipeline is being replaced by End-to-End Speech
   Language Models (SpeechLMs).
•  By processing audio directly, SpeechLMs enable real-time,
   full-duplex interaction and preserve vital paralinguistic
   cues like pitch and tone.
•   Early voice assistants treated tone as noise, losing all
    affective.

                                                                                                          28

visualInspection.notes: All summary bullets inspected. Repeats rule/retrieval/generation evolution, intent/context, SpeechLM shift, full duplex and affective cues; no new code or numerical premise. Existing qualifications on historical scope and guarantees carry forward.
